lessons.title: Installing Throttle Assembly
lessons.body: Start by gathering your tools: a 4mm and 5mm Allen key, a 10mm spanner, electrical tape, and a multimeter. You'll also need the throttle assembly that matches your handlebar diameterâmost EV bikes use a 22.2mm bar, so check before you buy. Begin by sliding the throttle grip onto the right side of the handlebar. It should move freely without binding. If it's tight, lightly sand the bar with 400-grit paper. Next, position the throttle housing so the cable exit points downward, away from rain and dust. Tighten the two housing screws evenlyâdon't overtighten or you'll crack the plastic. Now route the throttle cable along the handlebar, using the existing clips or zip ties. Keep the cable away from sharp edges and hot parts. For EVs, the throttle is usually a hall-effect sensor, so there's no physical cable to the motorâjust a wire. But some kits still use a cable to a potentiometer. Identify which type you have. If it's a hall sensor, you'll have three wires: 5V, ground, and signal. Connect them to the controller's throttle input, usually a 3-pin connector. If it's a potentiometer, you'll have three wires as well, but check the resistance: typically 0-5k ohms. Solder or crimp the connections, then insulate with heat shrink. Test the throttle by turning the key on and measuring voltage at the signal wire. At rest, it should be around 0.8V; at full twist, about 4.2V. If you get no change, recheck your wiring. Finally, secure the throttle housing with a locknut if provided. Make sure the grip doesn't rub against the brake lever or switch housing. Spin the handlebar left and right to ensure no pulling on the wires. A well-installed throttle should snap back to idle when released. If it sticks, lubricate the grip with silicone spray, not oil, which attracts dust. In Africa, dust is your enemy, so use rubber boots on connectors. Test ride at low speed in a safe area before full power.

lessons.title: Connecting Throttle to Controller
lessons.body: The controller is the brain of your EV motorbike. It takes the throttle signal and sends power to the motor. Connecting the throttle correctly is criticalâwrong wiring can fry the controller or cause dangerous full-throttle runaway. First, locate the controller. It's usually a metal box under the seat or near the battery. Find the throttle connector. Most controllers have a 3-pin plug labeled 'throttle' or 'speed control'. If not, check the wiring diagram. The three pins are typically: red (5V), black (ground), and green or white (signal). Your throttle will have matching wires. Use a multimeter to confirm: set to DC volts, probe red and blackâyou should get 5V with the key on. If not, the controller may need a different voltage or is faulty. Now, connect the throttle's 5V to controller 5V, ground to ground, and signal to signal. Never reverse 5V and groundâit will destroy the hall sensor. If your throttle has a switch for reverse or cruise, those are separate wires; connect them according to the controller's manual. Some controllers have a 'learning' mode: twist the throttle fully and hold while turning on the key, then release. This calibrates the throttle range. After connecting, turn on the key and slowly twist the throttle. The motor should respond smoothly. If it jerks or stutters, check for loose connections or interference. Keep throttle wires away from high-current motor cablesâthey can induce noise. Use shielded cable if needed. If the motor runs at full speed without touching the throttle, immediately disconnect the battery. That means the signal wire is shorted to 5V or the controller is set for a different throttle type. You may need to program the controller for 'hall' vs 'potentiometer'. Many controllers have a programming port or Bluetooth app. In Africa, where support may be limited, always test with a small fuse (5A) in the battery line to prevent damage. Once working, secure all connectors with heat shrink and zip ties. Label the wires for future troubleshooting. A proper connection ensures reliable acceleration and long controller life.

lessons.title: Mounting Handlebar Controls
lessons.body: Handlebar controls include the throttle, brake levers, switches for lights, horn, and turn signals, and sometimes a display. Proper mounting keeps you safe and comfortable. Start by cleaning the handlebar with a rag and alcohol. Mount the left switch cluster first. Slide it on, but don't tighten yet. Position it so your thumb can reach the buttons without moving your hand from the grip. The horn button should be closest to the grip, then turn signals, then lights. Use a 4mm Allen key to snug the clamp. Next, install the brake levers. Most EV bikes use a brake lever with a built-in switch that cuts power to the motor when you brake. That's a safety featureânever bypass it. The lever should have two wires; connect them to the controller's brake input (usually a 2-pin connector). Adjust the lever angle so your fingers rest comfortablyâabout 15 degrees below horizontal. Now mount the right switch cluster, but leave room for the throttle. The throttle goes on first, then the switch cluster. Ensure the throttle grip doesn't rub against the switch housing. Tighten the throttle housing screws evenly. Next, install the display if you have one. It usually mounts near the left grip. Route its cable along the handlebar with the others. Use zip ties every 10cm to secure the cables, but leave a little slack near the steering head so they don't pull when you turn. Test all controls: press the horn, check lights, turn signals, and brake switch. The brake switch should click when you squeeze the lever. If not, adjust the switch position or replace it. For off-road bikes, consider handguards to protect levers. In dusty conditions, use dielectric grease on all connectors. Finally, sit on the bike and check that you can reach all controls without stretching. Adjust as needed. A well-organized handlebar reduces fatigue and prevents accidents.

lessons.title: Adjusting Throttle Response
lessons.body: Throttle response is how quickly the motor reacts when you twist the grip. A jerky response can cause wheel spin, especially on loose surfaces like sand or gravel. A sluggish response makes the bike feel unresponsive. Most EV controllers have adjustable parameters: throttle curve, acceleration rate, and maximum current. If your controller has a programming interface (often a USB cable or Bluetooth app), you can change these. Start by setting the throttle curve to 'linear' or 'progressive'. Linear means the motor power increases evenly with twist. Progressive gives more power at the end of the twist, which is good for climbing. For beginners, linear is safer. Next, adjust the acceleration rate. This is how fast the controller ramps up power. A slow ramp (1-2 seconds) is gentle; a fast ramp (0.2 seconds) is aggressive. In Africa, where roads can be slippery, set a moderate ramp of 0.5 seconds. Also set the maximum current to match your battery and motor. If your motor is 1000W and battery is 48V, max current should be about 20A. Too high and you'll overheat; too low and you'll lack power. If your controller doesn't have programming, you can adjust the throttle mechanically. Some throttles have a set screw that limits how far you can twist. Turn it in to reduce full throttle, which softens response. You can also add a resistor in series with the signal wire to reduce voltage at full twist. For example, a 1k ohm resistor will lower the max signal from 4.2V to about 3.5V, reducing top speed and acceleration. Test ride in a safe area. Start slow, then gradually increase. Listen to the motorâif it whines or stutters, the response is too aggressive. Adjust and retest. Keep a notebook of settings that work for different terrains. In sandy areas, use a softer response; on tarmac, a sharper one. Always ensure the throttle returns to zero when released. A sticky throttle is dangerous. Lubricate the grip with silicone spray and check the spring tension. If the spring is weak, replace the throttle assembly.

lessons.title: Installing Side Stand Sensor
lessons.body: A side stand sensor is a safety device that cuts power to the motor when the side stand is down. This prevents you from riding off with the stand down, which can cause a crash. Most EV controllers have a two-wire input for the side stand switch. The switch is usually a simple on/off mechanism: when the stand is down, the switch is closed (or open, depending on design), sending a signal to the controller to disable the motor. First, locate the side stand. It's bolted to the frame near the left footpeg. Remove the stand if necessary to access the mounting area. The sensor is often a small switch with a plunger that gets pressed when the stand is up. Install the switch so that when the stand is up, the plunger is pressed in. When down, the plunger extends. Use the bracket provided; if not, make one from 2mm aluminum plate. Secure with M5 bolts. Now wire the switch. Typically, one wire goes to ground, the other to the controller's side stand input. Check your controller manual for the correct polarity. Some controllers require the switch to be closed to ground to allow motor operation; others require an open circuit. Use a multimeter to test: with the stand up, check continuity between the two switch wires. It should be either open or closed. Then connect to the controller. If your controller doesn't have a dedicated input, you can wire the switch in series with the throttle signal wire. When the stand is down, the switch opens the circuit, cutting the throttle signal. This is a simple and effective method. After wiring, test: turn on the key, put the stand down, and twist the throttle. The motor should not spin. Then put the stand up and twistâmotor should run. If it works opposite, reverse the switch logic by using a normally closed switch or adding a relay. In dusty conditions, the switch can get clogged. Clean it with compressed air and apply dielectric grease. Check it monthly. A faulty side stand sensor can leave you stranded, so carry a bypass wire in your tool kit. But never ride with the stand downâit's dangerous.

lessons.title: Testing Control Inputs
lessons.body: Before you ride, you must test every control input to ensure they work correctly. This includes throttle, brake switches, side stand sensor, and any other switches like reverse or cruise. Start with a visual inspection: check all connectors are tight, wires are not pinched, and no bare wires are touching the frame. Use a multimeter set to continuity or DC volts. First, test the throttle. Turn on the key. Measure voltage at the controller's throttle signal wire (usually green or white) with the throttle released. It should be around 0.8V. Slowly twist to full and watch the voltage rise to about 4.2V. If it jumps or drops, the throttle is faulty. Next, test the brake switches. Squeeze the front brake lever. You should hear a click from the switch. Measure voltage at the controller's brake inputâit should change from 0V to 5V (or vice versa). Do the same for the rear brake. If no change, adjust the switch or replace it. Now test the side stand sensor. Put the stand down. Twist the throttleâthe motor should not spin. Put the stand upâmotor should spin. If not, check the switch wiring. Test the reverse switch if you have one. Engage reverse and slowly twist the throttleâthe motor should spin backwards. Be careful: reverse can be powerful. Test the lights, horn, and turn signals. For the horn, press the buttonâit should sound clearly. For turn signals, check all four corners. If a light doesn't work, check the bulb and connections. Finally, test the kill switch if equipped. It should cut power to the motor. After testing, take a short ride in a safe area. Start at low speed and test each control in motion. Brake hard to test the cut-off. If any control fails, fix it before riding on roads. Keep a log of test results and dates. In Africa, where roads can be rough, regular testing prevents breakdowns. A simple 10-minute check before each ride can save your life.

quiz.q: What is the typical handlebar diameter for most EV motorbikes?
quiz.explanation: Most EV motorbikes use a 22.2mm handlebar, which is standard for many bicycles and small motorcycles.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for tightening the throttle housing screws?
quiz.explanation: Throttle housing screws are typically 4mm Allen bolts, so a 4mm Allen key is the correct tool.

quiz.q: What should you use to lubricate a sticky throttle grip?
quiz.explanation: Silicone spray lubricates without attracting dust, unlike oil or grease.

quiz.q: How many wires does a hall-effect throttle typically have?
quiz.explanation: A hall-effect throttle has three wires: 5V, ground, and signal.

quiz.q: What voltage should you measure at the throttle signal wire at rest?
quiz.explanation: At rest, the throttle signal is typically around 0.8V, rising to about 4.2V at full twist.

quiz.q: What happens if you reverse the 5V and ground wires on a hall-effect throttle?
options: D) The motor runs at full speed
quiz.explanation: Reversing 5V and ground will destroy the hall-effect sensor.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the controller's 'learning' mode?
options: A) To teach you how to ride
B) To calibrate the throttle range
quiz.explanation: Learning mode calibrates the throttle so the controller knows the full range of the signal.

quiz.q: What should you do if the motor runs at full speed without touching the throttle?
quiz.explanation: This indicates a short or wrong throttle type, and disconnecting the battery prevents damage or injury.

quiz.q: Why should throttle wires be kept away from high-current motor cables?
options: D) To make them last longer
quiz.explanation: High-current cables can induce noise in the throttle signal, causing erratic motor behavior.

quiz.q: What is the recommended fuse size for testing a new controller connection?
quiz.explanation: A small 5A fuse protects the controller during initial testing if there is a wiring fault.

quiz.q: Which control should be closest to the grip on the left switch cluster?
quiz.explanation: The horn button should be closest to the grip for quick access without moving your hand.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the brake lever switch?
options: A) To turn on the brake light
B) To cut power to the motor when braking
quiz.explanation: The brake switch cuts power to the motor when the brake is applied, preventing acceleration while braking.

quiz.q: How often should you secure cables along the handlebar with zip ties?
quiz.explanation: Zip ties every 10cm keep cables tidy and prevent them from snagging.

quiz.q: What should you apply to connectors in dusty conditions?
quiz.explanation: Dielectric grease protects connectors from dust and moisture without conducting electricity.

quiz.q: What is a good acceleration ramp setting for slippery roads?
quiz.explanation: A 0.5-second ramp provides a balance between responsiveness and traction on slippery surfaces.

quiz.q: If your motor is 1000W and battery is 48V, what is the approximate maximum current?
quiz.explanation: Power equals voltage times current, so 1000W / 48V â 20.8A, rounded to 20A.

quiz.q: What does a 1k ohm resistor in series with the throttle signal wire do?
quiz.explanation: The resistor drops the voltage, reducing the maximum signal and thus top speed and acceleration.

quiz.q: What should you do if the throttle does not return to idle when released?
options: B) Lubricate the grip and check spring tension
quiz.explanation: A sticky throttle is dangerous; lubricating the grip and checking the spring can fix it.

quiz.q: How is the side stand sensor typically wired to the controller?
options: A) In series with the battery
B) To a dedicated input or in series with throttle signal
quiz.explanation: The side stand sensor connects to a dedicated input or in series with the throttle signal to cut motor power.

quiz.q: What should happen when the side stand is down and you twist the throttle?
options: C) Motor spins at full speed
quiz.explanation: The side stand sensor should cut power to the motor when the stand is down.

quiz.q: How can you test a side stand switch with a multimeter?
options: A) Measure voltage at the battery
B) Check continuity between switch wires
C) Measure resistance of the motor
quiz.explanation: Continuity testing shows whether the switch is open or closed when the stand is up or down.

quiz.q: What is a safe alternative if your controller lacks a side stand input?
options: B) Wire the switch in series with the throttle signal
C) Connect it to the brake light
quiz.explanation: Wiring the switch in series with the throttle signal cuts the signal when the stand is down, disabling the motor.

quiz.q: What should you carry in your tool kit in case the side stand sensor fails?
quiz.explanation: A bypass wire lets you override a faulty side stand sensor to get home, but never ride with the stand down.

quiz.q: When testing control inputs, what should you check first?
quiz.explanation: A visual inspection catches loose connectors or pinched wires before electrical testing.

quiz.q: What voltage change should you see at the brake input when squeezing the brake lever?
quiz.explanation: Typically, the brake switch sends 5V to the controller when the brake is applied.

quiz.q: How can you test the reverse function safely?
options: B) At low speed in a safe area
quiz.explanation: Reverse can be powerful, so test at low speed in a safe area to avoid accidents.

quiz.q: What should you do if a turn signal does not work?
options: B) Check the bulb and connections
quiz.explanation: Most turn signal issues are due to a burnt bulb or loose connection.

quiz.q: Why is it important to test controls before every ride?
options: B) To prevent breakdowns and accidents
quiz.explanation: Regular testing catches problems early, ensuring safety and reliability.

quiz.q: What should you do if the kill switch does not cut power?
quiz.explanation: A faulty kill switch is a safety hazard and must be fixed before riding.

quiz.q: What is the best way to document your control tests?
options: B) Keep a log with dates and results
quiz.explanation: A written log helps track issues and ensures regular maintenance.
